content: Proto-oncogene tyrosine-protein kinase Fyn, also referred to as p59-FYN, Slk, Syn, or MGC45350, is an enzyme encoded by the FYN gene in humans. Fyn is a 59-kilodalton member of the Src family of kinases, which are primarily involved in T-cell and neuronal signaling during development and in maintaining normal cellular physiology. Disruptions in these signaling pathways are often implicated in the development of various cancers. As a proto-oncogene, Fyn encodes proteins that regulate cell growth. However, mutations or alterations in its DNA sequence can transform it into an oncogene, leading to the production of an aberrant protein that disrupts normal cellular regulation. Fyn is a membrane-associated tyrosine kinase that plays a role in controlling cell growth. It interacts with the p85 subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and binds to the fyn-binding protein. Additionally, alternative splicing of FYN transcripts results in distinct isoforms of the protein. Fyn belongs to the Src family of kinases (SFK), which was the first proto-oncogene family to be identified. The discovery of SFKs in 1976 earned J. Michael Bishop and Harold E. Varmus the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1989. Fyn itself was first identified in 1986 and was initially referred to as Syn or Slk, based on probes derived from v-yes and v-fgr. A hallmark of SFKs is their frequent upregulation in cancers. Fyn is functionally distinct from other members of the Src family due to its interactions with focal adhesion kinase (FAK) and paxillin (PXN), which are critical for regulating cell morphology and motility. Fyn is a tyrosine-specific phosphotransferase that is part of the Src family of non-receptor tyrosine kinases, which also includes Abl, Src, Janus kinase, and focal adhesion kinase. Fyn is a key component of the integrin signaling pathway, where it activates the Ras signaling cascade. It is located downstream of several cell surface receptors and is particularly associated with neuronal development and T-cell signaling. Upon activation, Fyn triggers downstream molecular signals that are essential for cellular growth and motility. Fyn is predominantly localized to the cytoplasmic side of the plasma membrane, where it phosphorylates tyrosine residues on target proteins. This phosphorylation either regulates the activity of the target protein or creates binding sites that recruit other signaling molecules. Fyn also functions as a tumor suppressor under normal conditions. However, when its normal activity is disrupted, Fyn can contribute to the transformation of normal cells into cancerous ones, progressing from pre-invasive stages to invasive cancer and ultimately metastasis. Understanding the role of Fyn in normal cellular signaling is critical for elucidating its involvement in cancer, as cancer often arises from the dysregulation of these pathways. Identifying the signaling pathways that involve Fyn is essential for developing pharmacological agents to mitigate uncontrolled signaling. Several tools have been instrumental in studying Fyn's role in specific signaling systems. These include cells derived from Fyn-deficient (Fyn-/-) mice, as well as cells from triple knockout mice lacking Fyn, Src, and Yes (SYF mice). Additionally, a kinase-inactive, dominant-negative mutant form of Fyn (K299M) and pharmacological inhibitors of Src family kinases, such as PP2, have been used. However, it is important to note that PP2 also inhibits other tyrosine kinases, including Abl, PDGFR, and c-Kit. Using these tools, Fyn has been shown to play a role in various signaling pathways, including T-cell and B-cell receptor signaling, integrin-mediated signaling, growth factor and cytokine receptor signaling, platelet activation, ion channel function, cell adhesion, axon guidance, fertilization, mitotic entry, and the differentiation of natural killer cells, oligodendrocytes, and keratinocytes. Fyn interacts with a wide range of proteins, including ADD2, BCAR1, C-Raf, CBLC, CD36, CD44, CDH1, CHRNA7, CTNND1, CBL, CSF1R, DLG4, dystroglycan, EPHA8, FYB, FASLG, GNB2L1, GRIN2A, ITK, Janus kinase 2, KHDRBS1, Lck, LKB1, nephrin, PAG1, PIK3R2, PRKCQ, PTK2B, PTK2, PTPRT, UNC119, RICS, SH2D1A, SKAP1, Syk, TNK2, TRPC6, tau protein, TrkB, TYK2, TUBA3C, WAS, and ZAP-70. The Src family of kinases, including Fyn, is closely associated with cancer progression, particularly in processes such as invasion, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, angiogenesis, and metastasis. Fyn’s normal role in cellular growth and proliferation can be co-opted to promote cancer cell progression and metastasis. Overexpression of Fyn has been shown to induce morphological transformation in normal cells and enhance anchorage-independent growth, a hallmark of cancer. Fyn overexpression has been implicated in several cancers, including prostate cancer, glioblastoma multiforme, squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, pancreatic cancer, chronic myelogenous leukemia, and melanoma. In prostate cancer, Fyn overexpression promotes the anti-apoptotic activity of Akt, allowing cancer cells to evade normal cell death pathways. In glioblastoma multiforme, Fyn and Src act as effectors of oncogenic EGFR signaling, driving tumor invasion and cancer cell survival. Fyn’s normal roles in cell migration and adhesion are exploited by cancer cells to facilitate growth and metastasis. For example, Fyn interacts with integrins, which are cell surface receptors that mediate communication with the extracellular matrix, and FAK, a tyrosine kinase involved in directed cell movement. Dysregulation of these pathways enables cancer cells to alter their shape and motility, increasing their invasive and metastatic potential. Other pathways involving Fyn that are under investigation include the Rac and Rho family of GTPases, Ras, Erk, and MAPK signaling cascades. Given its central role in cancer progression, Fyn has become a target for anti-cancer therapeutic research. Inhibition of Fyn, like other Src family kinases, reduces cell growth. Expression of a kinase-dead Fyn (KD-Fyn), which competes with endogenous Fyn, has been shown to reduce the size of primary tumors in mice. Targeting Fyn’s unique properties, along with inhibiting FAK and PXN, holds promise for developing effective combination therapies for cancer. Additionally, Fyn inhibitors are being explored as potential treatments for Alzheimer’s disease.
